chapters.title: Chapter 6: Putting Forex Knowledge to Work

lessons.title: Case Study: A Tiruppur Garment Exporter Hedges a $2 Lakh Order

children.text: Meena Sundaram runs a mid-sized knitwear unit in Tiruppur, India's knitwear capital, with about 180 workers. In early January 2026, a European fashion retailer confirms an order for cotton T-shirts worth $200,000, which Tiruppur exporters casually call a "two lakh dollar order." Delivery is due in March and payment at the end of April. Her margin is thin, her costs are in rupees, and the next four months will turn out to include a record low for the rupee, heavy RBI intervention and one of the sharpest one-day rupee rallies in years. This case study walks through Meena's decisions step by step, using everything from this course: exposure mapping, natural hedges, forwards, options, the rules on hedging and, finally, an honest look at whether the hedge was worth it.

body.text: A good hedging decision is made before the market moves, sized to the real exposure, and judged by whether it protected the business's margin, not by whether it beat the exchange rate in hindsight.

This is an illustrative composite case. Meena, her company and her buyer are fictional. Exchange rates are simplified and illustrative, though the direction of the rupee's moves follows the broad pattern of early 2026.

children.text: The Order and the Margin

stats.label: Target profit
stats.context: 12% of the order's rupee value at 90.00

body.caption: Meena's costs for the order, budgeted at USD/INR 90.00

cells: Cotton yarn from Tamil Nadu spinning mills
Imported specialty dyes and finishing chemicals

children.text: At 90.00, the order brings in ₹1,80,00,000 against costs of ₹1,58,40,000, leaving ₹21,60,000, a 12% margin. Meena knows from experience that a few rupees' move in USD/INR can wipe out half of that. Her first job is not to guess the rupee's direction. It is to work out exactly how much currency risk she really has.
Step 1: Map the Exposure and Use the Natural Hedge

The $12,000 of imported dyes will be paid in dollars in March. Meena keeps export proceeds from earlier orders in her EEFC account and pays the dye supplier from it, so those dollars never pass through the rupee. That leaves a net exposure of $200,000 minus $12,000 = $188,000 to be converted into rupees, against rupee costs of ₹1,47,60,000.

body.title: Meena's budget rate
body.prompt: Meena must convert her net $188,000 into rupees and has rupee costs of ₹1,47,60,000. What average USD/INR rate does she need on the $188,000 to earn exactly her target profit of ₹21,60,000? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Rupees needed = ₹1,47,60,000 + ₹21,60,000 = ₹1,69,20,000. Rate needed = ₹1,69,20,000 ÷ $188,000 = 90.00. That is her budget rate: any hedge at or above 90.00 protects her planned margin. Her break-even rate, with zero profit, is ₹1,47,60,000 ÷ $188,000 = 78.51.

body.label: Meena's hedging benchmark
body.value: Budget rate of 90.00 on a net $188,000
body.context: Every hedging choice is judged against this rate and the ₹21,60,000 target profit, not against what the rupee does later.

children.text: Step 2: Build a Layered Hedge

Meena's unit has a written hedging policy: hedge at least half of a confirmed order immediately, protect part of the rest with options if premiums are reasonable, and decide on the remainder within two months. With a forward premium of about 2.5% a year, a four-month forward is available at around 90.75, above her budget rate.

cells: Bank forward with an option period for delivery
90.65, delivery any day from 15 April to 15 May
Locks most of the margin; flexible delivery date covers buyer delays
Bought USD/INR put option from her bank
Strike 90.00, premium ₹0.50 per dollar, expiry 30 April
Sets a floor near the budget rate but keeps the upside
Left open, to be reviewed by mid-March
Allows her to benefit if the rupee weakens, within a limited share of the order

body.title: Why an option-period forward, and why not NSE futures?

markDefs.definition: A bank forward contract that lets the customer deliver the foreign currency on any day within an agreed window, instead of one fixed date, usually at a slightly less favourable rate.

children.text: Buyers rarely pay on the exact due date. A fixed-date forward would force Meena to find dollars on 30 April even if her buyer paid two weeks late. An
option-period forward
lets her deliver any day in a window, in return for a slightly lower rate, 90.65 instead of about 90.75.

She also considered selling USD/INR futures on NSE, which is permitted because she has a genuine exposure. But futures come in fixed monthly expiries and require daily mark-to-market cash. If the rupee weakened sharply, her short futures would demand lakhs of rupees in daily debits months before the export money arrived. For a small business whose working capital is already tied up in yarn and wages, the bank forward, secured against her existing credit limit, was the better fit.

body.title: The cost of the put
body.prompt: Meena buys a USD/INR put on $40,000 with a premium of ₹0.50 per dollar. How much premium does she pay in January, in rupees?
body.explanation: Premium = ₹0.50 × 40,000 = ₹20,000. That is the maximum cost of Layer 2. If the rupee strengthens below 90.00, the put pays out; if not, she loses only the ₹20,000 and converts at the better market rate.

children.text: Step 3: The Four Months That Tested the Plan

events.title: Order confirmed and hedged
events.description: Meena books the $110,000 option-period forward at 90.65 and buys the $40,000 put at a strike of 90.00. She records both against the buyer's purchase order.

events.title: Production and a delay request
events.description: The buyer asks to pay two weeks late, around mid-May. Her option-period forward already covers delivery until 15 May.

events.title: Rupee slides; Layer 3 is locked
events.description: With crude rising and FPIs selling, USD/INR reaches about 94.80. Following her policy deadline, Meena books a forward on the remaining $38,000 for mid-May at 95.40, well above her budget rate. She ships the goods and pays the dye supplier from her EEFC account.

events.title: Record low for the rupee
events.description: The rupee touches a record low near 95.2 against the dollar. Meena's open risk is now zero: every dollar of her net exposure is hedged or protected.

events.title: RBI measures and a sharp rally
events.description: After RBI's curbs on bank positions and rupee NDFs, the rupee jumps to about 93.10 in a day. Unhedged exporters who had waited for 96 or 97 see the rate move sharply against them.

events.title: Put expires
events.description: USD/INR is about 93.40, above the 90.00 strike, so the put expires unused. Its job was insurance against a much stronger rupee, which did not happen.

events.title: Payment arrives
events.description: The buyer pays $200,000. Meena delivers $110,000 under Layer 1 at 90.65, delivers $38,000 under Layer 3 at 95.40, converts $40,000 at the spot rate of 93.60, and keeps $12,000 in EEFC to replace the dollars used for the dyes.

Less: put premium paid in January

body.latex: \text{Effective rate} = \frac{\text{Total rupees received}}{\text{Net dollars}} = \frac{1{,}73{,}20{,}700 \text{ rupees}}{188{,}000 \text{ dollars}} = 92.13
body.caption: Meena's blended rate across all three layers, after the option premium

body.title: Meena's final profit
body.prompt: Meena received ₹1,73,20,700 for her net $188,000, and her rupee costs were ₹1,47,60,000. What was her profit on the order, in rupees?
body.explanation: Profit = ₹1,73,20,700 minus ₹1,47,60,000 = ₹25,60,700. That is ₹4,00,700 above her ₹21,60,000 target, because two layers were hedged above her 90.00 budget rate and part of the order kept some upside.

children.text: Step 5: Was the Hedge Worth It?

In hindsight, Meena would have earned more by not hedging at all, because the rupee ended weaker than 90.00. But hedging decisions are made in January, not in May. To judge the plan fairly, compare it with what could have happened if the rupee had gone the other way, say to 87.00 by the payment date, with the put paying out and Layer 3 left open.

body.caption: Meena's profit under two possible rupee paths (rupee costs ₹1,47,60,000)

children.text: Layer 1 forward: $110,000 × 90.65 = ₹99,71,500, unchanged.
Layer 2 put: converting $40,000 at 87.00 gives ₹34,80,000, the put pays (90.00 minus 87.00) × 40,000 = ₹1,20,000, and the premium was ₹20,000, so ₹35,80,000 net.
For simplicity, this assumes the put's settlement and the payment both happen at 87.00. In practice the put would settle at its own expiry rate on 30 April.

body.text: Meena gave up about ₹2.76 lakh in the world that actually happened, and gained about ₹5 lakh of protection in the world that could have happened. Her hedged profit stayed between roughly ₹21 lakh and ₹25.6 lakh across both paths, while the unhedged profit swung between ₹16 lakh and ₹28.4 lakh. That narrowing of outcomes is exactly what a hedge is for. A business that needs to pay 180 workers and a yarn supplier every month values the certainty more than the extra upside.

Meena's plan works because every hedge matched a real order and she never hedged more than her net exposure. Two 2026 realities matter for any exporter copying it. First, RBI restricted rebooking of cancelled rupee derivative contracts in April 2026, so cancelling a forward to chase a better rate may not be reversible. Second, rupee-pair contracts must always be backed by genuine exposures. Check current rules with your bank before booking, extending or cancelling hedges.

body.title: Judging the hedge
body.question: Meena's accountant says: "The rupee ended at 93.60. We lost money by hedging at 90.65." What is the best response?
options: He is right; the company should stop hedging future orders
The hedge did its job: it secured a profit above the ₹21,60,000 target, and it would have protected the business if the rupee had strengthened instead
The company should have sold twice the order value forward to make more money
Hedging is only worthwhile if it beats the spot rate at payment
body.explanation: Hedges are judged against the budget rate and the margin they protect. Meena beat her target profit and narrowed the range of outcomes. Judging a hedge against the final spot rate leads businesses to stop hedging just before the move that hurts them. Over-hedging would have been speculation, and is not permitted for rupee-pair derivatives.

body.title: Meena's next order
body.scenario: It is mid-September 2026. The same retailer offers Meena a $300,000 order for spring, with payment due in late February 2027. USD/INR is about 95.50, near record lows. Her rupee costs have risen with yarn prices. She has $15,000 of dollar costs for imported chemicals. Her budget rate, the rate needed for a 12% margin, works out to 93.20. Crude is above $100, FPIs are selling, the Fed meets on 16 September, and RBI holds large forward commitments. A fellow exporter says: "The rupee is at a record low, it has to bounce back. Hedge everything now." Another says: "It will go to 100, stay open."
body.prompt: Using the steps from this case study and course, design Meena's hedging plan for the new order: net exposure, benchmark, layers, tools, timing around events and rules to follow. Explain why neither exporter's advice should drive the decision.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Net exposure: $300,000 minus $15,000 of dollar costs paid from the EEFC account = $285,000.
2. Benchmark: the budget rate of 93.20. Spot at 95.50 and forwards, which will carry a forward premium on top, are well above it, so hedging now locks in a margin comfortably above target on the hedged portion.
3. Layers: for example, forward 50% to 60% immediately with an option-period forward covering possible payment delays; buy puts on 20% to 25% to keep some upside while setting a floor near the budget rate; and leave the remaining 15% to 30% to be decided by a fixed date, such as mid-November, whatever the rupee does.
4. Timing: the Fed decision on 16 September lands at 11:30 pm IST, so booking the core forward before it removes the event risk on that layer. Option premiums may also rise around big events.
5. Tools: bank forwards for the core, because they fit her cash flow and credit lines; options for flexibility. NSE futures would add daily mark-to-market cash demands.
6. Rules: hedge only against the confirmed purchase order, never more than $285,000; keep records; and remember that cancelled contracts may not be rebookable under RBI's 2026 rules.
7. Neither exporter's advice should drive the decision. One is a forecast that the rupee must bounce, the other a forecast that it will fall further. Nobody can reliably call either. Meena's policy, based on her budget rate, net exposure and layers, protects the margin in both worlds, which is the only goal a hedge is designed to meet.

body.title: The exporter's hedging playbook from this course
steps: Map the order: amount, currency, delivery and payment dates.
Net off natural hedges such as dollar costs paid from the EEFC account.
Calculate the budget rate that delivers the target margin.
Hedge a core share immediately, using flexible delivery if payment dates may slip.
Use options on part of the exposure to keep upside, if premiums are reasonable.
Set a firm deadline for the open portion and stick to it.
Check event dates like RBI and Fed decisions in IST before booking.
Never hedge more than the net exposure, keep records, and check current RBI rules before cancelling or rebooking.
Judge the result against the budget rate, not the spot rate on payment day.

body.title: The flexible forward
body.textWithBlank: A bank forward that lets an exporter deliver dollars on any day within an agreed window is called an option-___ forward.
body.explanation: An option-period forward gives flexibility on the delivery date, which helps when buyers pay earlier or later than planned, usually at a slightly less favourable rate than a fixed-date forward.

cards.definition: Foreign currency receipts minus foreign currency payments that can be matched. $200,000 minus $12,000 = $188,000 for Meena.
The exchange rate that delivers the target margin. 90.00 for Meena's first order.
A bank forward with a delivery window instead of a single date.
Combining forwards, options and a timed open portion to balance protection and upside.
Total rupees received divided by net dollars, including option premiums. 92.13 for Meena.
The real test of a hedge: how much it narrows the gap between the best and worst possible results.

points: Start every hedge by mapping the real exposure and netting off natural hedges, like Meena's $12,000 of dollar costs paid from her EEFC account.
Calculate a budget rate that delivers the target margin, and judge every hedge against it.
Layer the hedge: a core forward, options for part of the exposure, and a firm deadline for the rest.
Choose tools that fit the business: option-period forwards handle payment delays, while futures' daily mark-to-market can strain a small exporter's cash.
Meena's plan earned ₹25.6 lakh, above target, and would have earned about ₹21 lakh if the rupee had strengthened to 87.00, against ₹16 lakh unhedged.
A hedge is worth it when it narrows the range of outcomes around the margin the business needs, even if hindsight shows a better rate.
Hedge only genuine exposures, never more than the net amount, and check RBI's current rules on documentation, cancellation and rebooking.

body.text: This case study is for education only and is not hedging, investment, accounting, tax or legal advice. The business, buyer, costs and exchange rates are illustrative. Bank products, pricing and RBI rules on hedging change over time. Exporters and importers should design hedging policies with their bank, chartered accountant and qualified advisers.
